title: Double Integrals over General Regions
description: Double integrals over non-rectangular regions: sweep a slice across a region to see the inner limits move, Type I and Type II descriptions, Fubini on a slanted solid, switching the order, decomposing regions, and area and average value.

steps.label: Beyond Rectangles
steps.subtitle: The inner limits can depend on the outer variable
steps.bodyHtml:
Last lesson every region was a rectangle \(R=[a,b]\times[c,d]\), so every limit of integration was a constant. Most regions are not rectangles: a disk, a triangle, the sliver between two curves. We call such a region \(D\), and we still want \(\displaystyle\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA\), the volume over \(D\) under \(z=f(x,y)\).

The disk \(x^2+y^2\le4\). Press Sweep, or drag the slice. The red segment is one slice of \(D\); the red shading is the part of \(D\) swept so far.

Watch where the slice starts and stops as it moves. How is that different from a rectangle?

On a rectangle the slice always runs between the same two numbers. On \(D\) its endpoints move, so the inner limits are functions of the outer variable. The outer limits stay constants.

steps.label: Definition
steps.subtitle: Type I and Type II regions
steps.bodyHtml:
Type Ibetween two vertical lines and two curves \(y=g_1(x)\), \(y=g_2(x)\):
\(D=\{(x,y)\mid a\le x\le b,\;g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x)\}\)
Type IIbetween two horizontal lines and two curves \(x=h_1(y)\), \(x=h_2(y)\):
\(D=\{(x,y)\mid c\le y\le d,\;h_1(y)\le x\le h_2(y)\}\)

Example 5.11. The region in the first quadrant between \(y=\sqrt{x}\) and \(y=x^3\). Switch between the two sweeps: Type I slices are vertical, Type II slices are horizontal.

Where do the curves meet?\(\sqrt x=x^3\Rightarrow x=0\) or \(x=1\), so the outer limits are \(0\) and \(1\) in either order
Type I description\(0\le x\le1,\;x^3\le y\le\sqrt x\). The bottom curve is \(y=x^3\), the top is \(y=\sqrt x\).
Type II descriptionSolve each curve for \(x\): \(y=\sqrt x\Rightarrow x=y^2\), \(y=x^3\Rightarrow x=\sqrt[3]{y}\). So \(0\le y\le1,\;y^2\le x\le\sqrt[3]{y}\).

Tip: sketch the region and draw one slice. The curve the slice enters through is the lower limit, the one it leaves through is the upper limit.

steps.label: Fubini's Theorem for General Regions
steps.subtitle: Theorem 5.4 and a solid with a slanted face
steps.bodyHtml:
If \(f\) is continuous on \(D\), the double integral is an iterated integral whose inner limits come from the region:

$$\text{Type I:}\quad\iint_D f\,dA=\int_a^b\!\!\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x,y)\,dy\,dx,\qquad \text{Type II:}\quad\iint_D f\,dA=\int_c^d\!\!\int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x,y)\,dx\,dy.$$

Example 5.17. The tetrahedron bounded by \(x=0\), \(y=0\), \(z=0\) and the plane \(2x+3y+z=6\). Its floor is the triangle \(D\) below the line \(2x+3y=6\), and its roof is \(z=6-2x-3y\). Top: the solid, cut by a plane. Blue: the cross-section. Below: its area \(A(x)\) and the volume collected so far. Sweep it, then switch to the other order.

Describe \(D\) as Type I\(0\le x\le3,\;0\le y\le 2-\tfrac23x\)
Cross-section area at fixed \(x\)\(\displaystyle A(x)=\int_0^{2-2x/3}(6-2x-3y)\,dy=\tfrac23(3-x)^2\)
Add up the cross-sections\(\displaystyle V=\int_0^3\tfrac23(3-x)^2\,dx=\tfrac23\cdot9=\mathbf{6}\)
Does the other order agree?Yes. Type II: \(\displaystyle\int_0^2\!\!\int_0^{3-3y/2}(6-2x-3y)\,dx\,dy=6\). The same solid, sliced the other way.

steps.label: Example 5.12
steps.subtitle: Evaluating a Type I integral: \(\displaystyle\iint_D x^2e^{xy}\,dA\)
steps.bodyHtml:
\(D=\{0\le x\le2,\;x/2\le y\le1\}\), a triangle. Sweep once to see why the lower limit moves but the upper limit does not.

Set up\(\displaystyle\int_0^2\!\!\int_{x/2}^{1}x^2e^{xy}\,dy\,dx\)
Inner integral (treat \(x\) as constant)\(\displaystyle\int_{x/2}^1x^2e^{xy}\,dy=\Big[x\,e^{xy}\Big]_{y=x/2}^{y=1}=xe^{x}-xe^{x^2/2}\)
Outer integral\(\displaystyle\int_0^2\left(xe^x-xe^{x^2/2}\right)dx=\Big[xe^x-e^x-e^{x^2/2}\Big]_0^2=(2e^2-e^2-e^2)-(-1-1)=\mathbf{2}\)
Why not Type II?It is legal (\(0\le y\le1,\;0\le x\le2y\)), but then the inner integral is \(\int x^2e^{xy}\,dx\), which needs integration by parts twice. The order was chosen for the integrand.

steps.label: Switching the Order
steps.subtitle: When one order cannot be done at all: \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_x^1 e^{y^2}\,dy\,dx\)
steps.bodyHtml:
The integral \(\int e^{y^2}\,dy\) has no elementary antiderivative, so the inner step in the order given is a dead end. The fix is to read the region off the limits, then describe the same region the other way.

Start on Type I (the order given: \(0\le x\le1,\;x\le y\le1\)). Then switch to Type II and sweep again.

The regionThe triangle with vertices \((0,0)\), \((0,1)\), \((1,1)\), under the line \(y=1\) and above \(y=x\)
Rewrite as Type II\(0\le y\le1,\;0\le x\le y\), so \(\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^{y}e^{y^2}\,dx\,dy\)
Inner integral\(\displaystyle\int_0^ye^{y^2}\,dx=ye^{y^2}\), since \(e^{y^2}\) is constant in \(x\)
Outer integral\(\displaystyle\int_0^1ye^{y^2}\,dy=\Big[\tfrac12e^{y^2}\Big]_0^1=\mathbf{\dfrac{e-1}{2}}\)

Order of steps: sketch the region from the limits, redraw the slice the other way, read the new limits, then integrate.

steps.label: Theorem 5.5
steps.subtitle: Decomposing a region
steps.bodyHtml:
If \(D=D_1\cup D_2\) with the pieces overlapping only along a boundary, then \(\displaystyle\iint_D f\,dA=\iint_{D_1}f\,dA+\iint_{D_2}f\,dA\). Use it when \(D\) is not Type I or Type II as a whole, but is a union of pieces that are.

The L-shaped region below has a top edge that jumps at \(x=1\), and a Type I description needs \(g_2\) to be continuous. Cut it at the dashed line.

Evaluate \(\displaystyle\iint_D(x+y)\,dA\) over this L.

\(D_1\)\(0\le x\le1,\;0\le y\le2\)
\(D_2\)\(1\le x\le2,\;0\le y\le1\)
\(\displaystyle\iint_{D_1}(x+y)\,dA\)\(\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^2(x+y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1(2x+2)\,dx=3\)
\(\displaystyle\iint_{D_2}(x+y)\,dA\)\(\displaystyle\int_1^2\!\!\int_0^1(x+y)\,dy\,dx=\int_1^2\left(x+\tfrac12\right)dx=2\)
Add them\(3+2=\mathbf{5}\)

steps.label: Area and Average Value
steps.subtitle: Using \(f=1\), and dividing by the area
steps.bodyHtml:
Taking \(f(x,y)=1\) makes the volume over \(D\) equal to its base area:

$$A(D)=\iint_D 1\,dA,\qquad f_{\text{ave}}=\frac{1}{A(D)}\iint_D f(x,y)\,dA.$$

Example 5.18. The area bounded below by \(y=x^2\) and above by \(y=2x\) in the first quadrant.

The curves meet at \(x=0\) and \(x=2\). \(\displaystyle A=\int_0^2\!\!\int_{x^2}^{2x}dy\,dx=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx=\mathbf{\tfrac43}\).

Example 5.19. The average value of \(f(x,y)=7xy^2\) over the region between \(x=y\) and \(x=\sqrt y\).

Area of \(D\)\(\displaystyle\int_0^1(x-x^2)\,dx=\tfrac12-\tfrac13=\tfrac16\)
The double integral\(\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_{x^2}^{x}7xy^2\,dy\,dx=\tfrac73\int_0^1(x^4-x^7)\,dx=\tfrac73\cdot\tfrac{3}{40}=\tfrac{7}{40}\)
Average value\(\dfrac{7/40}{1/6}=\mathbf{\dfrac{21}{20}}\)

steps.label: Problems from the Text
steps.subtitle: OpenStax Section 5.2 (Checkpoints and Example 5.15)
steps.bodyHtml:
Sketch the region, set up the iterated integral, evaluate, then reveal.

#ProblemAnswer
Checkpoint 5.11\(\displaystyle\iint_D(x^2+y^2)\,dA\) where \(D\) is the first-quadrant region between \(y=2x\) and \(y=x^2\).\(\displaystyle\int_0^2\!\!\int_{x^2}^{2x}(x^2+y^2)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^2\left(\tfrac{14}{3}x^3-x^4-\tfrac13x^6\right)dx=\mathbf{\tfrac{216}{35}}\). Type II gives the same number.
Checkpoint 5.14The average value of \(f(x,y)=xy\) over the triangle with vertices \((0,0)\), \((1,0)\), \((1,3)\).\(D=\{0\le x\le1,\;0\le y\le3x\}\), \(A=\tfrac32\). \(\displaystyle\iint_D xy\,dA=\int_0^1\tfrac92x^3\,dx=\tfrac98\). Average \(=\mathbf{\tfrac34}\).
Example 5.15Reverse the order and evaluate \(\displaystyle\int_0^{\sqrt2}\!\!\int_0^{2-x^2}xe^{x^2}\,dy\,dx\).Region: \(0\le y\le2,\;0\le x\le\sqrt{2-y}\). \(\displaystyle\int_0^2\!\!\int_0^{\sqrt{2-y}}xe^{x^2}dx\,dy=\tfrac12\int_0^2\left(e^{2-y}-1\right)dy=\mathbf{\tfrac12(e^2-3)}\).
Checkpoint 5.12The volume under \(f(x,y)=10-2x+y\) over the region \(0\le x\le1,\;0\le y\le e^x\).\(\displaystyle\int_0^1\!\!\int_0^{e^x}(10-2x+y)\,dy\,dx=\int_0^1\left[(10-2x)e^x+\tfrac12e^{2x}\right]dx=\mathbf{\tfrac{e^2+40e-49}{4}}\approx16.78\).

steps.label: Summary and What Comes Next
steps.subtitle: The one-page version
steps.bodyHtml:
Region typesType I: \(a\le x\le b,\;g_1(x)\le y\le g_2(x)\). Type II: \(c\le y\le d,\;h_1(y)\le x\le h_2(y)\).
ComputingInner limits are functions of the outer variable; outer limits are constants. The result is a number.
Choosing an orderSketch \(D\) and one slice. Pick the order that keeps the limits simple and the integrand integrable. Switch by redescribing \(D\).
PiecesIf \(D\) is not Type I or II, cut it into pieces that are, and add the integrals.
Usesarea \(\iint_D1\,dA\), volume under \(f\), average value \(\frac{1}{A(D)}\iint_Df\,dA\)

Not covered today, in the same section of the text: improper double integrals (unbounded regions, Theorems 5.6 and 5.7) and joint probability densities (Examples 5.22 and 5.23). Next lesson: regions like the disk we started with are far easier in polar coordinates.
